The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 is deeply flawed, particularly its stapling provisions that could default three million workers into underperforming funds and its unprecedented directions power giving the Treasurer authority to cancel private sector investments. Labor will move amendments to prevent stapling to underperforming funds and to reject the directions power.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 unfairly targets industry super funds, which have outperformed retail funds (30% asset growth since 2018 versus 3.2%), and that Labor is seeking amendments to protect workers' retirement savings from excessive red tape, regulatory uncertainty, and an ideological attack.

The bill would require employers to check existing super funds via the ATO when a new employee does not nominate one, mandate annual APRA performance tests for funds, and prohibit persistently underperforming funds from accepting new members after two years, with the aim of saving Australians $14 billion over a decade. It also clarifies trustees’ obligations to act solely in members’ financial interests.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 gives the Treasurer unilateral power to cancel investments, a measure the speaker called illiberal and dangerous, and argued it fails to reduce superannuation fees while potentially locking up to three million Australians into underperforming funds costing $635,000 less in retirement.

The speaker supported schedules 1 and 2 of the bill—which staple super accounts to employees and introduce annual performance testing—but opposed schedule 3, arguing its “best financial interests” covenant, reversal of the burden of proof, and regulation-making power allowing the Treasurer to ban investments could harm members and were not recommended by reviews. They called on the government to rethink schedule 3 and re-engage with stakeholders.

The independent MP announced they will oppose the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, primarily because schedule 3 gives the Treasurer broad unilateral powers over super fund investments; they support other schedules subject to amendments including delaying stapling until after two years of performance testing and applying the performance test to all funds equally.

The Morrison government's Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 aims to save Australians $17.9 billion over 10 years by limiting multiple superannuation accounts, requiring annual performance tests for super products, and tightening trustee duties to act in members' best financial interests.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 for introducing a single default fund, transparency on underperforming funds, and a best-interest duty, and argued Labor opposed it to protect union funding and influence.

The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, arguing it would allow workers to be stapled to underperforming superannuation funds, replace trustees’ duty to act in members’ best interests with a narrower “best financial interests” standard that could discourage long-term community investments, and give the Treasurer excessive power via unfinished regulations—reflecting what the speaker described as a government ideological attack on industry superannuation, despite industry funds outperforming retail funds and the royal commission finding widespread abuse in retail funds only.

The speaker gave qualified support for the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, urging amendments such as sequencing to eliminate poor-performing funds before the stapling provision begins, extending annual performance tests to all superannuation products not just MySuper, and setting a financial threshold on best‑financial‑interest provisions to avoid unnecessary administrative costs. They welcomed the removal of the directions power and specifically opposed the use of compulsory superannuation for political donations, advertising at sporting events, or corporate box hire.

The Morrison government's Your Future, Your Super Bill implements Productivity Commission and banking royal commission recommendations to prevent multiple super accounts, empower member choice, penalise underperforming funds, and increase transparency, projected to save Australians nearly $18 billion over 10 years.

The government introduced the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (International Production Orders) Bill to create a framework for independently authorised cross-border data requests from designated communications providers, enabling a bilateral CLOUD Act agreement with the United States and reciprocal assistance for partner countries. The bill includes safeguards such as provider objection rights, oversight by the Commonwealth Ombudsman and Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security, and annual ministerial reports to parliament.

The speaker supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (International Production Orders) Bill 2020, noting the government agreed to 23 bipartisan amendments from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, but criticised the Morrison government for being slow to negotiate a CLOUD Act agreement with the United States and accused the Prime Minister of falsely claiming the bill lacked bipartisan support.

The Greens argued that the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (International Production Orders) Bill 2020 lacks adequate protections and safeguards, including for human rights, journalists' data, and parliamentary scrutiny, with critical details left to future international agreements and concerns about the Administrative Appeals Tribunal issuing orders instead of the judiciary.

The speaker opposed the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (International Production Orders) Bill 2020, arguing it was being rushed through Parliament without adequate debate. They noted that over 80 national security laws have been passed since 9/11 and called for the bill to be delayed until the next day for full consideration.

The bill creates a framework for international production orders to obtain electronic data from foreign communications providers, aiming to reduce delays in international cooperation for serious crime investigations, and its passage is a critical step to finalising a bilateral CLOUD Act agreement with the United States.
